title: Built a crypto paper trading bot. What am I missing before I trust the results?
author: drebels
selftext:
Hello yall 🙋🏼‍♂️

I got interested in trading recently and spent the last few days researching and building a bot. I’m new to this, so I’d appreciate a reality check from people who have tested their own systems.

Right now the bot runs in paper mode and monitors BTC/USDT, ETH/USDT, and SOL/USDT on the 1-hour chart. SOL/USDT was the initial focus, and I’m tracking the other two pairs as well on the 1-hour chart. The strategy uses RSI, MACD, EMA 20/50, a volume filter, ATR-based stops and targets, a trailing stop, and a cooldown between trades. It risks 1% of the simulated account per trade.

I also built a monitoring dashboard and added market news through n8n, so I can review what the bot saw and why it made a decision. My plan is to run it on paper for at least 3–6 weeks and inspect the trades before even considering a small live account. I’m not assuming the bot “learns” just by running. I want to use the data to find mistakes and test any changes properly.

What would you check first? I’m especially interested in whether my testing period is too short, how you account for fees and slippage, and what would convince you that a strategy has an actual edge rather than a few lucky trades.

There’s enough room for people to share useful advice here, so if you’ve made beginner mistakes building a bot, I’d like to hear them.

comments.author: Cool_Big2955
comments.body:
hey man welcome to the rabbit hole! your setup sounds way  more solid than most beginners tbh. running paper for 3-6 weeks is smart but honestly its still pretty short for crypto. i’d say aim for at least 2-3 different market regimes (one big dump, one sideways chop, one pump) before going live. if you only test in a bull run you wont know if your stops actually work when volatility spikes.

here’s what i’d check first based on my own misstakes:

slippage and fees are brutal. in paper trading everything fills perfect. in real life especially with SOL which can move fast you might get slipped 0.5-1% easily  make sure your backtests/paper logs deduct at least 0.1% per trade (taker fee) + estimated slippage. if your edge is small this will kill you

volume filter is key  , i use a hard rule: no trade if 24h volume < $50M. saves you from getting stuck in low liquidity coins where you cant exit without crashing the price.

atr vs fixed stops. glad you using atr. fixed % stops get wrecked in crypto. but make sure your trailing stop isnt too tight initially. i start with 2x atr for crypto (3x for stocks) then tighten to 1.5x and 1.2x as profit grows. prevents getting shaken out by normal noise.

anchor entries matter. dont just buy because rsi is low. wait for price to stabilize above a recent low (like 3 closes above the 48h box low).. this "anchor" logic prevents catch,ing falling knives. let the market prove the bottom is in before you enter.

"edge" vs luck. to prove edge dont just look at total profit. look at profit factor (gross profit / gross loss). if its under 1.5 you probably just got lucky. also check max drawdown. if your bot made 20% but had a 40% drop at some point its too risky for real money.

my biggest beginner mistake was letting ai "decide" trades in real time. now i keep execution deterministic (hardcoded rules) and only use ai offline to score closed trades and tweak params slowly. keeps things fast and predictable.

keep inspecting those n8n logs! seeing why it took a trade is worth more than the trade itself. good luck!

comments.author: profittoinvest
comments.body:
I’d go much further back than 3–6 weeks before trusting anything. If you can, test the same logic back to 2020 so you see how it behaves across very different market regimes — bull runs, long downtrends, sideways periods, high-volatility crashes and especially trend transitions.

Those transition periods are often where a strategy that looks great in one regime suddenly gets hurt, so I’d inspect them separately instead of only looking at total return.

At the same time, keep a paper or very small live account running with exactly the same rules. Then compare live results with the backtest: fills, slippage, missed trades, drawdown, win rate, average trade, etc. If they diverge too much, that usually tells you something in the backtest assumptions is too optimistic.

Personally I’d want at least 3–6 months of forward results before trusting it with meaningful capital. And when you start changing parameters, keep part of the historical data untouched as out-of-sample, otherwise it’s very easy to optimize the bot to the past instead of finding a real edge.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
first thing I'd check is trade count, not weeks. on the 1-hour chart with a cooldown, 3 to 6 weeks is maybe 20 to 40 trades across three pairs, and that many trades cannot separate a real edge from a lucky month no matter how carefully you inspect them. the period is done when you have a few hundred, which on 1h bars means either a long wait or backtesting the same rules over the last couple of years first.

fees: charge the taker fee on both sides plus half the spread, and put the slippage on the stop, not the entry. stops fill worse than entries because you're hitting a market that's moving against you.

what convinces me a rule has something: the neighbours agree. RSI 12, 14 and 16 with EMA 18/45 and 22/55 should all look roughly the same. if only your exact settings work, you found the settings, not an edge. and run the same stops and targets on random entry times as a control.

beginner mistake I made: trailing stop computed on candle close in the backtest, triggered on the wick live. that alone flipped a result.

comments.author: tradematesHQ
comments.body: Your stack is RSI, MACD, EMA 20/50, volume filter, ATR stops  -  that's basically every YouTube bot ever built, so the edge isn't in the indicators, it's in how it behaves when the regime flips. 3-6 weeks of paper is one market mood, not a test. You need a dump, a chop, and a pump minimum, ideally backtested to 2020 so you see trend transitions where these strategies quietly bleed. Fees and slippage will eat a 1-hour crypto strategy alive if you're trading often  -  model them at realistic taker rates before you believe any equity curve. The real question isn't 'is it profitable', it's 'is it profitable after costs across three regimes', and most bots fail that one.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
Good breakdown above — the regime-diversity point is the one that matters most. One thing worth adding on top of it: since the bot pulls in market news through n8n for context, worth checking whether that news ingestion is actually timestamped and used causally — i.e., the bot's decision at each bar only sees news that had actually published by that point, not news your review dashboard shows you in hindsight. It's an easy thing to get subtly wrong in a paper-trading loop, and it inflates apparent edge in exactly the way that only shows up once you're live and the news arrives after price already moved.

On what would convince me of a real edge: not the aggregate return, but whether the bot's win rate and average R stay roughly consistent when you slice the paper period into weekly chunks rather than looking at the whole curve — a real edge should look boringly similar week to week; a lucky run usually has 2-3 outlier weeks carrying the entire result. That slice test is cheap to run and catches "few lucky trades" faster than waiting out more calendar time.

The event-timing discipline here — making sure your bot only ever reacts to information genuinely available at that timestamp — is exactly the guarantee EventTrader's data pipeline is built to enforce, since news/event lag is one of the most common ways a paper-trading result quietly overstates what'll happen live.https://claude.ai/artifact/VuwYE2KYrtzMdwyEpvA9wH

comments.author: lambardar
comments.body:
test regimes. 

how will the bot react if the market went up tomorrow.. or if it went tits up.

are you ready to commit? 

  
3-6 weeks is nothing. crypto is not that cyclic but like a stretched square wave. 

sol was down to $10 a few years ago.. what does your strategy do in that scenario?

comments.author: CODE_HEIST
comments.body:
i'd add failure tests before more indicators. restart while a simulated position is open, replay the same signal twice, and disconnect the price feed while a trailing stop is active. check whether positions, stops and cooldowns recover exactly as intended.



does the dashboard distinguish a deliberate no-trade decision from a missed update? a clean equity curve won't show you that difference by itself.
